Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
A specific temperature on the skin

Maladaptive Strategies.value: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows
I work hard at keeping busy with other things

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

vignette: Omar, a 48-year-old fashion designer from a Middle Eastern background, was working in his loft studio on a brisk November morning when the city's air-conditioner burst into flames. The blast sent shards of glass raining down, the roar of the fire filling the small space, and a sudden, unbearable heat that scorched his skin. He was trapped in the cramped room, unable to escape before the door locked from the inside. In that split second, his world collapsed into a blur of smoke, frantic cries, and the oppressive weight of impending doom. The memory of that instant is the seed from which every subsequent symptom grew. When the intrusive memory of the fire flares-triggered by a sudden flash of bright light or the hiss of a draft-Omar immediately feels a wave of nausea and a chill that settles on his skin, as if the temperature from that night is replaying in his body. The nausea forces him to drop a sketchbook and, in a panic, to stab the heel of his left shoe with a sewing needle. He knows this self-harm cuts through the overwhelming flood of emotion, offering a brief, jarring relief. The same flash also sets off his instinct to map escape routes, drawing lines on his notebook, and to repeatedly check every lock, door, and window in the studio, as if the world could still close itself off in a second. His busy work schedule becomes an anchor; he immerses himself in patterns of draping and cutting, hoping the rhythm will drown out the intrusive images. The fragmented pieces of the fire haunt Omar in a way that feels both disjointed and alive. He can taste the metallic tang of the burning air whenever the memory surfaces, a vivid reminder that the event is not past but ongoing. The sudden appearance of this taste acts as a trigger that brings the memory back into focus, and the memory's return, in turn, sharpens his vigilance. He scans the studio, eyes darting to every corner, every seam, every potential threat, because the feeling of danger is so palpable. The memory's intensity also pushes him to self-harm again, to check the locks, and to stay busy with his design work, as these acts become ritualistic defenses against the flood of recollection. Omar's heightened threat perception-the constant mental cartography of escape routes, the ceaseless checking of locks, and the hyper-focus on possible danger-reinforces the cycle. Every time he checks a door, a memory of the moment the lock failed and the door wouldn't open resurfaces, confirming his belief that the world could lock him in again. The relentless scanning, too, brings flashes of the fire's roar, the taste of burning fabric, and the nauseous chill, solidifying the connection between perceived threat and memory recall. He feels the need to maintain this surveillance, lest a new threat trigger the same cascade of terror. When Omar resorts to self-harm, the physical act does not just provide temporary relief; it jolts him back into the memory of the fire, as if the pain reopens a fissure in his mind. The act of hurting himself then heightens his sense of threat-each cut and each checked lock becomes evidence of how precarious his safety feels. His frantic need to keep busy, to create patterns and textures, is no longer simply a distraction but a defensive attempt to keep the threat from crossing the threshold into memory again. Each loop tightens: the triggers prompt the maladaptive strategies; the strategies feed the memory and the sense of threat; the threat, in turn, reinforces the strategies. It was the cumulative weight of missed deadlines, strained relationships with colleagues, and the constant fear that his studio's walls might once again close in on him that finally pushed Omar to seek help. He fears that, if he does not break this cycle, the memory of that fire will continue to haunt his body, taste, and every moment of his life, turning his creative world into a battleground where he can never rest. Yet he also hopes that, with professional support, he can reclaim the studio's bright mornings and the freedom to design without the shadow of that night lingering in his thoughts.
